opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of control theory and reinforcement learning less as rivals and more as two ends of a spectrum. Control theory gives us a beautiful toolkit for when we know a lot about the system ahead of time: we have a model of the dynamics, we can reason about stability, and we can make guarantees. That's incredibly valuable, especially when a machine is physically attached to a person.

The world, though, rarely holds still for our models. In my own work on prosthetic limbs and other assistive technologies, every person is different. The same person is different from morning to evening, the socket fit changes, their muscles tire, their goals shift. A controller tuned perfectly in the lab can start to drift the moment someone walks out the door. That's where reinforcement learning, and continual learning more broadly, comes in. It lets a system keep learning from its own stream of experience and adapt to the specifics of the situation it's actually in, rather than the one we imagined when we designed it.

The interplay I find most exciting is prediction. Before a system can control well, it helps a lot if it can anticipate what's about to happen: where the user's arm is going, what signal is coming next, what the consequences of an action will be. We've done a lot with learned predictions, things like general value functions, where the system is constantly forecasting many aspects of its world. Those predictions can feed directly into fairly simple control rules, almost reflex-like, and you get surprisingly adaptive behaviour without having to learn a full policy from scratch.

So in practice I see a layered picture. Classical control provides the safe, well-understood foundation: low-level loops, safety limits, the things you really don't want to relearn on the fly. Learning sits on top and around it, building predictions, tuning parameters, and gradually taking on more of the decision-making as it earns trust. And critically, the human is part of that loop too. The person and the machine are both learning about each other, and the best systems I've seen are the ones designed for that kind of partnership, not just autonomous optimization.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prosthetic limbs and changing user or device conditions, but does not identify controlling robots that radically change their physical form as a difficult control theory problem.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning from ongoing experience to adapt systems, with reinforcement learning layered on classical control and safety mechanisms.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of the two as really complementary, and in some ways they're trying to solve the same problem from different directions. Control theory gives us this beautiful, principled machinery for stabilizing a system and making it behave the way we want, but it tends to lean on having a good model of the plant and the environment up front. Reinforcement learning comes at it from the other side: it says, let's assume we don't have that model, or that the world is going to shift under us, and let's learn from the stream of experience as it comes in.

Where that gets really interesting for me is in the systems I work with most, which are prosthetic limbs and other devices that have to work with a person. A prosthesis is a wonderful example of a system where the "environment" includes a human being who changes from day to day, whose muscles fatigue, whose goals shift minute to minute. You can't write down a single fixed controller that's going to be right forever. So what we've been doing is layering learning on top of control. The low-level control loops keep things safe, smooth, and predictable, and then reinforcement learning sits alongside them, continually making predictions about what's going to happen next and gradually adjusting how the device responds to the person.

A lot of my own interest is in that predictive piece. Methods like temporal-difference learning let a system build up thousands of little forecasts about its own sensors, about the user's signals, about what the next few seconds are likely to hold. Those predictions become a kind of knowledge about the world that the controller can then use. In a sense, the control-theoretic part provides the stability and the guarantees, and the learning part provides the adaptability and the ability to keep improving with a specific person over time.

I'd also say the field has a lot to gain by not treating these as rival camps. Adaptive control, model predictive control, and reinforcement learning share deep roots. What excites me is seeing people from both traditions sit down together and ask how we make systems that are both trustworthy and able to keep learning for a lifetime of interaction with the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prosthetic devices and changing human needs, but does not identify controlling robots that radically change their physical form as a difficult control-theory problem.

r002.rationale: It proposes layering reinforcement learning on top of low-level control loops, with learning from ongoing experience to adapt how the device responds.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Control theory gives us powerful ways to keep a system stable and make it behave predictably. Reinforcement learning gives us a way to improve behavior through experience, particularly when we can’t specify everything about the world in advance.

A prosthetic arm is a useful example. You need reliable control of the motors, but the person using that arm is changing, their goals are changing, and the situations they encounter are changing. Learning can help the device adapt to those changes, while a control system provides the foundation for dependable movement.

And the person is learning too. So the challenge isn’t just to build a machine that adapts to a fixed user. It’s to build a relationship in which the person and the machine can get better at working together. That’s where I think combining control and learning becomes especially interesting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a prosthetic arm adapting to a changing user and environment, but does not describe robots changing their physical form or identify that as a control theory challenge.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning can improve behavior through experience and help a prosthetic arm adapt, while a control system provides dependable movement.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as very complementary. Control theory gives us powerful ways to describe a system’s dynamics and reason about stability—how to keep a system behaving reliably. Reinforcement learning gives us a way to improve behavior through interaction, particularly when we don’t have a complete model of the world or when that world changes.

A prosthetic arm is a useful example. You need reliable control of the motors, but you also need to adapt to the person using it. Their intentions, their movements, and the tasks they’re trying to accomplish can all change. Learning can help the device anticipate what comes next and adjust its behavior, while control provides structure for turning those adaptations into dependable action.

The interesting question is how to put those pieces together so that adaptation happens continuously and usefully. The person is learning to use the device, and the device is learning about the person. We want that ongoing interaction to make the whole system more capable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a prosthetic arm and reliable motor control, but does not identify controlling robots that radically change physical form as a difficult control theory problem.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning can improve behavior through interaction and adaptation, while control theory provides structure for reliable action, communicating that learning from experience can improve systems governed by control.
